subject: feedback on line exception class design

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: feedback on line exception class design
parts:
I just wondered if anyone had any feedback on my
line exception class design before I dropped it into
the code generator and model includes.

Daniel --- I'm particularly interested in your feedback
here because it's relevant to your desire to have different
behavior based on the type of exception.

The reason I set it up this way was to allow:

* line number exceptions to be constructed using
a nested exception and line number

* allow original exception and line number to
be retrieved programatically (that's why it's using
BOTH inheritance and containment for e with
E(e) providing inheritance and e_(e) conainment.

* allow and exception to be caught by either the full
template class type for the line number exception
or the nested exception type (the latter is the the
hard part)

I'm particularly interested in hearing whether I

- implemented the destructor properly

- safely stored the nested exception by reference
properly (that is, got the scoping right)

- could somehow compute the what message lazily when
what() is called. I can't figure out how to do that
given the return type of const char* and I'd be creating
with a local variable; I wouldn't want to make what_ non-const
and set it, though that would be a viable lazy option

Also, I'm interested in whether people think it's
overengineered because it's going to be used in the
following way:

int line = -1;
try {
... do some work, update line, do some work, ...
} catch (std::exception& e) {
throw line_number_exception<std::exception>(e,line);
}

So the issue is that I'm only going to be using std::exception
to instantiate the nested type, though it'll be stored as is
and run-time type information could potentially extract its type.

So unless I modify the above to catch a variety of
exceptions and use them to create different template
parameters for line_number_exception, I won't get to use the
nested type for catching.

The alternative would be to just forego the template type
E and just hardcode it as std::exception. In that case, I
wouldn't need to call the superclass (copy) constructor E(e).

The following is a self-contained example. Compiling and
running produces this:

session
----------------------------------------

~/temp2$ clang++ exc.cpp
~/temp2$ ./a.out
caught it: exception raised at line=12: hello


exc.cpp
---------------------------------------

#include <exception>
#include <iostream>
#include <string>
#include <stdexcept>

template <class E>
class line_number_exception : public E {
private:
const int line_;
std::string what_;
const E& e_;

public:
line_number_exception(const E& e, int line) throw()
: E(e),
e_(e),
line_(line),
what_(std::string("exception raised at line=")
+ std::to_string(line)
+ std::string(": ")
+ std::string(e.what())) {
}

~line_number_exception() throw() {
}

const char* what() const throw() {
return what_.c_str();
};

const E& nested_exception() const {
return e_;
}

int line() const {
return line_;
}

};

int main() {
using std::domain_error;
domain_error err("hello");
line_number_exception<domain_error> lne(err,12);
try {
throw lne;
} catch (const domain_error& e) {
std::cout << "caught it: " << e.what() << std::endl;
} catch (...) {
std::cout << "missed" << std::endl;
}

}


Thanks.

- Bob

messages.author: 2a7f346506a3e9ff
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Re: feedback on line exception class design
parts:
The template pattern is really nice, but I'm not convinced it's worth it if you're not going to catch std::runtime_error and throw line_number_exception<std::runtime_error>.  The reason is that the pattern suggests that you should be able to catch a line_number_exception<special_exception_type> but that's only going to work if the model catches special_exception_type  and rethrows appropriately.  I.E., reasonably expected behaviour from the pattern will not work as expected which seems like a bad idea.

I see two possibilities:
1. Identify a short list of the exceptions that our code can throw and catch and rethrow explicitly.  Make it a policy that any functions to be used in models can *only* throw those kinds of exceptions.
2. Make a generic model_exception class which derives from std::exception.  Provide all the convenient RTTI/polymorphism features as functions of model_exception for when people care about exactly which exception was thrown.  E.G., have a model_exception::is_runtime_error() and model_exception::get_runtime_error().  This is almost what you have right now in effect but without the convenience functions since people would have to catch line_number_exception<std::exception> and then use RTTI to do anything more sophisticated than get the error message and line number.

Cheers,
Marcus

> On Mar 9, 2015, at 4:57 AM, Marcus Brubaker <marcus.a...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> The template pattern is really nice, but I'm not convinced it's worth it if you're not going to catch std::runtime_error and throw line_number_exception<std::runtime_error>.

That is what I'm going to do, but I think the "not"
in your sentence was a typo.

> The reason is that the pattern suggests that you should be able to catch a line_number_exception<special_exception_type> but that's only going to work if the model catches special_exception_type and rethrows appropriately. I.E., reasonably expected behaviour from the pattern will not work as expected which seems like a bad idea.

This is exactly what I was worried about, too. The
class works fine on its own and does as intended, but
the way I was planning to use it in try/catch blocks will
just catch std::exception (superclass of std::runtime_error)
and throw line_number_exception<std::exception>.

>
> I see two possibilities:
> 1. Identify a short list of the exceptions that our code can throw and catch and rethrow explicitly. Make it a policy that any functions to be used in models can *only* throw those kinds of exceptions.

If I do that, I can include long catch sequences and throw
the right kind of exception.

> 2. Make a generic model_exception class which derives from std::exception. Provide all the convenient RTTI/polymorphism features as functions of model_exception for when people care about exactly which exception was thrown. E.G., have a model_exception::is_runtime_error() and model_exception::get_runtime_error(). This is almost what you have right now in effect but without the convenience functions since people would have to catch line_number_exception<std::exception> and then use RTTI to do anything more sophisticated than get the error message and line number.

That's more along the lines of what I was thinking, though
rather than building that into the class, I'd just let users
grab a reference to the std::exception and have at it themselves.

Do you think it's worth building that in? I tend to not want
to build in generic functionality when it's accessible almost
as easily externally.

I could build it in generically with a pair of template
functions:

template <typename T>
bool is<T>() { ... }

template <typename T>
const T& get<T>() { ... }

...

> exec.cpp:19:20: error: no member named 'to_string' in namespace 'std'
> + std::to_string(line)
> ~~~~~^
> 1 error generated.
>
> StackOverflow appears to have some hits on this.
>
> This appears to fix it
>
> // + std::to_string(line)
> + static_cast<std::ostringstream*>( &(std::ostringstream() << line) )->str()

I'd either just use a stringstream everywhere (as we
do elsewhere to allow printing) or revert to C-style
strtoi(). I think I'll go with the stringstream because
it's a bit more C++-ey.

- Bob

messages.author: 2a7f346506a3e9ff
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Re: feedback on line exception class design
parts:
I think we're on the same page as to the options.  Option 1 puts a policy requirement on almost all Stan code for exceptions to work (functions can only throw a limited set of exceptions).  Option 2 complicates catching behaviour a bit.

Personally, I think policy should only be added if absolutely necessary because it makes it more difficult for people to write new, correct code.  As such, I would argue for option 2.


Cheers,
Marcus
